questions.question: For an ideal operational amplifier in the circuit shown in figure, the transfer function \(\dfrac{V_0(s)}{V_{\text{i}}(s)}\) is
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation:
For an ideal op-amp, \[V_{+}=V_{-}\] Since the non-inverting input draws zero current, \[V_{+}=V_{i}\] Hence, \[V_{-}=V_{i}\] Applying KCL at node \(a\), \[\frac{V_{i}}{R}+sC\left(V_{i}-V_{o}\right)=0\] Rearranging, \[sC\left(V_{o}-V_{i}\right)=\frac{V_{i}}{R}\] \[V_{o}=V_{i}\left(1+\frac{1}{sRC}\right)\] Therefore, the transfer function is \[\boxed{\frac{V_{o}(s)}{V_{i}(s)}=1+\frac{1}{sRC}
=\frac{1+sRC}{sRC}}\]

questions.question: The operational amplifier is used in the non linear mode in
questions.explanation: An operational amplifier operates in the non-linear mode when it is used without negative feedback or with positive feedback. In this mode, the output switches between the positive and negative saturation levels. A Schmitt trigger is a regenerative comparator that uses positive feedback, making it a non-linear application of the op-amp. \[\boxed{\text{(c) Schmitt triggers}}\]

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: To realize a phase shift oscillator,
options: It is possible to use a voltage follower as an amplifier along with a suitable phase shift network.
Only common emitter or common source stages can be used.
Given any phase shifting network, it is always possible to find the emitter follower.
questions.explanation: A phase shift oscillator must satisfy the Barkhausen criterion: \[|A\beta|=1,\qquad \angle A\beta=360^\circ\] The RC phase shift network provides a phase shift of \[180^\circ\] Therefore, the amplifier must contribute another \[180^\circ\] Only amplifiers that produce a \(180^\circ\) phase reversal, such as the common-emitter (BJT) or common-source (FET) configurations, can be used. A voltage follower or emitter follower provides zero phase shift and hence cannot sustain oscillations with an RC phase shift network. \[\boxed{\text{(b) Only common emitter or common source stages can be used}}\]

questions.question: The figure shown below is a common emitter amplifier. The component is wrongly placed because .
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation: In a voltage-divider biased common emitter amplifier, the biasing network (\(R_{1}\) and \(R_{2}\)) must be directly connected to the base to establish the required DC operating point. In the given circuit, the coupling capacitor \(C_{1}\) is placed between the bias network and the base. Since a capacitor blocks DC, the base becomes isolated from the biasing network and the transistor cannot be properly biased. Therefore, \(C_{1}\) is wrongly placed. It should be connected between the input source and the base-bias junction so that the AC signal is coupled while the DC bias remains unaffected. \[\boxed{\text{Component: }C_{1}\text{, because it blocks the DC bias to the base.}}\]

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: If the open loop transfer function of negative feedback control system is \(G(s)H(s) = \dfrac{K}{(s + 1)^3}\), then the gain \(K\) for a closed loop pole to be at \(\left( -\dfrac{1}{2} + j\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \right)\) is
questions.explanation:
The open-loop transfer function is given as \(G(s)H(s) = \dfrac{K}{(s + 1)^3}\). For a negative feedback control system, the characteristic equation is defined by \(1 + G(s)H(s) = 0\): \[(s + 1)^3 + K = 0\]
Method 1
Using the magnitude criteria, any point lying on the root locus must satisfy \(|G(s)H(s)| = 1\). \[\left| \frac{K}{(s + 1)^3} \right| = 1 \implies K = |s + 1|^3\] Substitute the value of the pole \(s = -\frac{1}{2} + j\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\): \[s + 1 = \frac{1}{2} + j\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\] \[|s + 1| = \sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^2} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{4} + \frac{3}{4}} = 1\] Therefore, the required gain value is: \[K = (1)^3 = 1\]
Method 2
Substitute the value of \(s\) directly into the characteristic equation: \[\left[\left(-\frac{1}{2} + j\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) + 1\right]^3 + K = 0 \implies \left(\frac{1}{2} + j\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^3 + K = 0\] Expressing \(\dfrac{1}{2} + j\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) in polar form: \(1 \cdot e^{j60^\circ}\). \[\left(1 \cdot e^{j60^\circ}\right)^3 + K = 0 \implies 1^3 \cdot e^{j180^\circ} + K = 0\] Since \(e^{j180^\circ} = -1\): \[-1 + K = 0 \implies K = 1\]
\[\boxed{\text{(A) 1}}\]
Key points
  • Magnitude Condition: For any valid pole on the root locus, \(|G(s)H(s)| = 1\).
  • Convert complex terms into phasor/polar form (\(r e^{j\theta}\)) to simplify higher power calculations easily.

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: A system has a complex pole pair of \((-1 \pm j2)\) and a real zero of \((-3)\). The steady state output to a unit step input is \(2\). The transfer function of the system is .
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation: Given a complex pole pair at \(s = -1 \pm j2\) and a real zero at \(s = -3\). The general form of the transfer function \(G(s)\) is: \[G(s) = \frac{k(s + 3)}{(s + 1 + j2)(s + 1 - j2)} = \frac{k(s + 3)}{(s + 1)^2 - (j2)^2} = \frac{k(s + 3)}{s^2 + 2s + 5}\] For a unit step input \(R(s) = \frac{1}{s}\), the steady-state output \(y_{ss}\) can be found using the Final Value Theorem: \[y_{ss} = \lim_{s \to 0} s \cdot Y(s) = \lim_{s \to 0} s \cdot G(s) \cdot \frac{1}{s} = G(0)\] Given that the steady state output is \(2\): \[G(0) = \frac{k(0 + 3)}{0^2 + 2(0) + 5} = 2 \implies \frac{3k}{5} = 2 \implies k = \frac{10}{3}\] Substituting \(k\) back into the expression for \(G(s)\): \[\boxed{G(s) = \frac{10(s + 3)}{3(s^2 + 2s + 5)}}\]

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: A unity feedback system has open loop poles \((-2 \pm j2)\) and \(0\). It has a single zero at \((-4 \pm j0)\). The angle of departure of the root locus branch starting from the pole \((-2 - j2)\) is
questions.explanation:
From the given \(s\)-plane diagram, the system has the following poles and zeros:
  • Poles at: \(P_1 = 0\), \(P_2 = -2 + 2j\), and \(P_3 = -2 - 2j\)
  • Zero at: \(Z_1 = -4\)
The angle of departure \(\phi_d\) at the complex conjugate pole \(P_2 (-2 + 2j)\) is given by the angle criterion: \[\phi_{d(-2 + 2j)} = 180^\circ - \sum \phi_p + \sum \phi_z\] \[\phi_{d(-2 + 2j)} = 180^\circ - (\phi_{p1} + \phi_{p3}) + (\phi_{z1})\] Where the individual angles contributed by the remaining poles and zeros to \(P_2\) are: \[\phi_{p1} = 180^\circ - \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2}{2}\right) = 135^\circ\] \[\phi_{p3} = +90^\circ\] \[\phi_{z1} = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2}{2}\right) = +45^\circ\] Substituting these values back into the expression: \[\phi_{d(-2 + 2j)} = 180^\circ - (135^\circ + 90^\circ) + 45^\circ = 0^\circ\] Since the root locus is symmetric about the real axis, the angle of departure at \(P_3 (-2 - 2j)\) is: \[\phi_{d(-2 - 2j)} = -\phi_{d(-2 + 2j)} = 0^\circ\] \[\boxed{0^\circ}\]

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: The asymptotic approximation to the log-magnitude versus frequency plot (Bode plot) of a unity feedback control system is shown in figure. The system is a minimum phase system. Determine the gain crossover frequency (in rad/sec), Gain margin (in dB) and Phase margin (in degrees).
questions.explanation:
From the Bode magnitude plot:
  • Initial slope is \(0\,\text{dB/dec}\).
  • At \(\omega_1\), the slope changes to \(-6\,\text{dB/octave}\) (\(=-20\,\text{dB/dec}\)), indicating a pole at \(\omega_1\).
  • At \(\omega_2=2\,\text{rad/s}\), the slope changes to \(-12\,\text{dB/octave}\) (\(=-40\,\text{dB/dec}\)), indicating another pole at \(\omega_2=2\,\text{rad/s}\).
Between \(\omega_1\) and \(\omega_2\), the magnitude decreases from \(20\,\text{dB}\) to \(12\,\text{dB}\). Hence, \[20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{\omega_2}{\omega_1}\right)=8\] \[20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{2}{\omega_1}\right)=8\] \[\omega_1=\frac{2}{10^{0.4}} \approx0.8\,\text{rad/s}\] Beyond \(\omega_2\), the slope is \(-40\,\text{dB/dec}\). The gain crossover frequency is obtained from: \[40\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{\omega_{c}}{\omega_2}\right)=40\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{\omega_{gc}}{2}\right)=12\] \[\omega_{gc}=2\times10^{0.3}\approx4\,\text{rad/s}\] Since the system is minimum phase, \[G(s)=\frac{K}{\left(1+\dfrac{s}{0.8}\right)\left(1+\dfrac{s}{2}\right)}\] The phase at the gain crossover frequency is: \[\angle G(j4) = -\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{4}{0.8}\right) -\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{4}{2}\right) =-78.69^\circ-63.43^\circ =-142.12^\circ\] \[\therefore\; \mathrm{PM} = 180^\circ-142.12^\circ \approx38^\circ\] Since the phase approaches \(-180^\circ\) only asymptotically, there is no finite phase crossover frequency. \[\therefore\quad \mathrm{GM}=\infty\] \[\boxed{(C)\;4,\;\infty,\;38^\circ}\]
Key points
  • \(6\,\text{dB/octave}=20\,\text{dB/decade}\).
  • Gain margin is infinite when the phase never reaches \(-180^\circ\) at any finite frequency.

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: A temperature control system is usually very sluggish. To improve its dynamics
options: a PI controller can be used
an I controller can be used
a PID controller with large I and a negligible D action can be used
a PD controller can be used
questions.explanation: Temperature control systems are generally slow due to their large thermal time constants. A proportional-derivative (PD) controller improves the transient response by providing anticipatory action, thereby increasing the speed of response without introducing integral-induced sluggishness. Hence, a PD controller is preferred for improving the dynamics of a sluggish temperature control system. \[\boxed{(D)\;\text{a PD controller can be used}}\]
